prompt_spec.original_prompt:
The role of phantasia and Erschlossenheit in disclosing the environment:
how Aristotle's account of phantasia in De Anima III.3 anticipates
Heidegger's concept of disclosedness (Erschlossenheit) in Being and Time.

Specifically address:
(a) How Aristotle's phantasia functions as the faculty that discloses appearances (phainomena),
(b) How Heidegger's Erschlossenheit structures the disclosure of Being-in-the-world,
(c) The structural parallel between these two modes of disclosure,
(d) Where the two frameworks diverge — Aristotle's faculty psychology vs. Heidegger's existential analytic.

Include verbatim quotations from both De Anima and Being and Time.
Target length: 1000-1500 words. Write as a single coherent section suitable for a doctoral dissertation.
research_questions: How does Aristotle's account of phantasia in De Anima III.3 anticipate Heidegger's concept of disclosedness (Erschlossenheit) in Being and Time?
How does Aristotle's phantasia function as the faculty that discloses appearances (phainomena)?
How does Heidegger's Erschlossenheit structure the disclosure of Being-in-the-world?
What are the structural parallels between Aristotle's phantasia and Heidegger's Erschlossenheit as modes of disclosure?
Where do Aristotle's faculty psychology and Heidegger's existential analytic diverge in their accounts of disclosure?

required_facets.name: Aristotle's Phantasia as Disclosure of Phainomena
required_facets.description: How does Aristotle theorize phantasia in De Anima Book III Chapter 3 as the psychological faculty that mediates between perception (aisthesis) and thought (noesis), enabling the disclosure of appearances (phainomena) to the soul? This facet examines Aristotle's definition of phantasia as distinct from both sensation and judgment, its role in making absent objects present to consciousness, its relationship to memory and imagination, and how phantasia functions as the condition for the possibility of thinking about objects not immediately present to the senses. Key passages include Aristotle's claim that phantasia is 'that in virtue of which an image occurs in us' and his analysis of how phantasia differs from perception, belief (doxa), and knowledge (episteme).

required_facets.name: Heidegger's Erschlossenheit and Being-in-the-World
required_facets.description: How does Heidegger develop the concept of Erschlossenheit (disclosedness or openness) in Being and Time as the fundamental existential structure through which Dasein's Being-in-the-world is constituted and made intelligible? This facet investigates Heidegger's analysis of disclosedness as comprising Befindlichkeit (state-of-mind or attunement), Verstehen (understanding), and Rede (discourse), and how these existential structures enable the disclosure of entities within-the-world and Dasein's own Being. Examine Heidegger's claim that Dasein is its disclosedness, the relationship between Erschlossenheit and truth (aletheia) as unconcealment, and how disclosedness precedes and grounds any particular acts of knowing or perceiving. Key sections include Being and Time paragraphs 28-34 and 44 on the existential constitution of the 'there' (Da) of Dasein.

required_facets.name: Structural Parallels: Mediation and Pre-Predicative Disclosu
required_facets.description: What are the structural and functional parallels between Aristotle's phantasia and Heidegger's Erschlossenheit as modes of disclosure that operate prior to explicit judgment and propositional knowledge? This facet examines how both concepts function as mediating structures that make entities accessible to consciousness or Dasein without reducing disclosure to either pure sensation or conceptual determination. Investigate the shared emphasis on pre-predicative or pre-theoretical access to beings, the role of absence and presence in both frameworks, how both concepts challenge strict subject-object dichotomies, and whether Heidegger's phenomenological retrieval of Greek philosophy explicitly or implicitly draws on Aristotelian phantasia. Consider secondary literature on Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotle, particularly his early Freiburg and Marburg lectures on Aristotle's psychology and ontology.

required_facets.name: Divergence: Faculty Psychology vs. Existential Analytic
required_facets.description: Where and how do Aristotle's faculty psychology and Heidegger's existential analytic fundamentally diverge in their accounts of disclosure, particularly regarding the ontological status of the disclosing agent, the metaphysical framework presupposed, and the methodological approach employed? This facet examines Aristotle's hylomorphic conception of the soul as the form of a living body with distinct faculties or powers (dynameis) versus Heidegger's rejection of substance ontology in favor of Dasein as existence (Existenz) whose Being is an issue for it. Analyze how Aristotle's phantasia remains within a representationalist framework where images mediate between external objects and internal mental states, while Heidegger's Erschlossenheit dissolves the inner-outer distinction through the concept of Being-in-the-world. Consider Heidegger's critique of traditional psychology and epistemology in Being and Time sections 12-13 and his destruction of the Cartesian ontology of the 'world'.

required_facets.name: Textual Evidence and Scholarly Reception
required_facets.description: What specific passages from De Anima III.3 and Being and Time provide the primary textual evidence for comparing phantasia and Erschlossenheit, and how have scholars in phenomenology, ancient philosophy, and comparative philosophy interpreted the relationship between these concepts? This facet focuses on gathering verbatim quotations in Greek and German with standard English translations, identifying the most relevant sections of both texts, and surveying secondary literature that explicitly addresses this comparison. Key scholarly works include Heidegger's own interpretations of Aristotle in his lecture courses, commentaries by scholars such as Theodore Kisiel, Thomas Sheehan, Franco Volpi, Walter Brogan on Heidegger's Aristotelianism, and ancient philosophy scholars who have engaged with phenomenological readings of Aristotle such as Victor Caston, Dorothea Frede, and Klaus Brinkmann.

claims.claim: Aristotle's phantasia functions as a mediating faculty that discloses appearances (phainomena) through a process of 'making-present-to-itself' that operates independently of immediate sensory presence, thereby enabling thought to engage with objects not currently perceived.
grounds: Heidegger characterizes Aristotelian thinking as 'not an appeal to a brain process, but to φαντασία, the "making-present-to-itself" of the world, in which what is made present is not actually there, but instead is, say, in memory.'
Aristotle's account acknowledges that 'theoretical reasoning cannot do without "images"' (phantasmata), indicating phantasia's indispensable role in cognitive operations.
Scholarly interpretations by Modrak and Nussbaum present 'competing but equally compelling readings of Aristotelian phantasia as a crucial part of the meaning-making process.'
claims.warrant: The characterization of phantasia as 'making-present-to-itself' reveals its function as a disclosure mechanism that transcends the immediate givenness of perception. By enabling the soul to engage with absent objects through retained images, phantasia establishes a mode of access to beings that is neither purely sensory nor purely intellectual, but mediates between these domains. This mediating function constitutes a form of disclosure because it makes phenomena available to consciousness in a way that enables further cognitive operations, particularly thinking and deliberation.
claims.backing: The necessity of images for theoretical reasoning demonstrates that phantasia is not merely auxiliary to cognition but constitutive of it. The scholarly recognition of phantasia's role in meaning-making further supports its status as a disclosure faculty rather than a passive repository of sensory residues.
claims.qualification: This interpretation depends on Heidegger's phenomenological reading of Aristotle, which may emphasize aspects of phantasia that Aristotle himself did not explicitly thematize as 'disclosure.'

claims.claim: Heidegger's Erschlossenheit structures the disclosure of Being-in-the-world by constituting Dasein as fundamentally characterized by λόγος, which governs how beings are 'uncovered' and 'exhibited' within the existential 'there' (Da) of Dasein's being.
grounds: Heidegger explicates 'the being-there of the human being as being-in-the-world, in such a way that λόγος came forth as the basic character of this being, determined as being-in: the how of this being.'
In Heidegger's framework, 'as λόγος is what governs, I draw my knowledge from hearing-saying,' indicating that disclosure operates through linguistic and interpretive structures.
The process of disclosure involves beings being 'uncovered, exhibited,' suggesting that Erschlossenheit is not passive reception but active unconcealment.
claims.warrant: By identifying λόγος as the 'basic character' of Dasein's Being-in-the-world, Heidegger establishes that disclosure is not a property or faculty of a subject but the very structure of Dasein's existence. The terms 'uncovered' and 'exhibited' (related to aletheia as unconcealment) indicate that Erschlossenheit is the condition for the possibility of entities showing themselves. This differs from a representational model where a subject apprehends external objects; instead, Dasein's Being is constituted by its openness to beings, and this openness is structured by λόγος as the articulative dimension of understanding.

claims.claim: Both Aristotelian phantasia and Heideggerian Erschlossenheit function as pre-predicative modes of disclosure that enable access to beings prior to explicit judgment, establishing structural parallels in their mediating roles between immediate presence and conceptual determination.
grounds: Aristotle's phantasia operates as 'making-present-to-itself' of what is 'not actually there,' functioning before propositional judgment.

Heidegger describes a mode of disclosure where 'there is for uncovering no possibility of dissimulating, of mis-leading,' suggesting a primordial access to beings that precedes the possibility of error inherent in propositional assertion.

Both frameworks position their respective disclosure mechanisms as mediating structures: phantasia between perception and thought in Aristotle, and Erschlossenheit as the existential condition for any particular acts of knowing in Heidegger.
claims.warrant: The structural parallel lies in how both concepts establish a level of disclosure that is more fundamental than propositional knowledge yet more articulated than mere sensation. Phantasia's 'making-present' of absent objects and Erschlossenheit's primordial 'uncovering' both describe modes of access that are not reducible to either pure receptivity or conceptual judgment. This pre-predicative character is crucial because it establishes the conditions for the possibility of truth and falsity in judgment—one cannot make true or false assertions about beings unless those beings are already disclosed in some way.

This aligns with phenomenological emphasis on pre-theoretical experience.

claims.claim: Aristotle's phantasia remains embedded within a faculty psychology that presupposes distinct powers (dynameis) of the soul, including the relationship between 'the appetitive power (ὀρεκτικόν)' as 'part of the sensitive power (αἰσθητικόν),' thereby maintaining a hylomorphic framework of soul-body unity.
grounds: Aristotle's analysis establishes that 'the appetitive power (ὀρεκτικόν) is part of the sensitive power (αἰσθητικόν) or that the possession of the sensitive faculty involves the possession' of appetite.

This framework involves 'a double type of consideration' regarding the soul (ψυχή), reflecting Aristotle's methodological commitment to analyzing the soul through its various faculties and their interrelations.

The concept of κίνησις as 'ἐντελέχεια, "presence," τοῦ δυνάμει ὄντος, "of a determinate being-there"' reveals Aristotle's metaphysical framework of potentiality and actuality structuring his account of psychic powers.
claims.warrant: Aristotle's faculty psychology operates within a substance ontology where the soul is understood as the form (eidos) of a living body, with distinct capacities or powers that are hierarchically organized and functionally differentiated. Phantasia, within this framework, is one faculty among others (perception, appetite, intellect), each with its proper object and operation. This commits Aristotle to a view where disclosure happens through the actualization of specific psychic powers in relation to their objects, maintaining a distinction between the soul as subject and the world as object, even while unified through hylomorphic composition.
claims.backing: The integration of appetite within the sensitive power demonstrates Aristotle's systematic approach to psychic faculties as interconnected yet distinct, each contributing to the soul's overall functioning. The potentiality-actuality framework further grounds this in a broader metaphysical system.

claims.claim: Heidegger's existential analytic fundamentally diverges from Aristotelian faculty psychology by rejecting substance ontology and reconceiving Dasein not as a being with properties or faculties but as existence whose Being is constituted by its 'being-there' (Da-sein), thereby dissolving the inner-outer distinction presupposed by representational models of disclosure.
grounds: Heidegger characterizes human existence as 'being-there' where 'the being whose being constitutes the τί ἤν εἶναι is designated as ἕκαστον, "the particular," the τί ἤν εἶναι constitutes the particularity of beings,' reinterpreting Aristotelian essence in existential terms.
The concept of Dasein as potentially 'become "no-longer-Being-there" [Nicht-mehr-da-sein]' emphasizes existence as temporal and finite rather than as a substance with enduring properties.

Heidegger's framework involves 'temporality' as fundamental, where 'to say that it is something which is "earlier" and "later", "not yet" and "no longer"' structures Dasein's Being, contrasting with Aristotle's atemporal account of psychic faculties.
claims.warrant: By reconceiving the human being as Dasein—literally 'being-there'—Heidegger shifts from asking 'what is the soul?' to 'how does Dasein exist?' This existential approach dissolves the subject-object framework that structures Aristotelian faculty psychology. Where Aristotle's phantasia mediates between an external world and an internal soul through images, Heidegger's Erschlossenheit is the very structure of Dasein's Being-in-the-world, eliminating the need for mediation. The emphasis on temporality as constitutive of Dasein's Being further distinguishes Heidegger's approach from Aristotle's analysis of timeless psychic capacities, making disclosure fundamentally historical and finite rather than a function of universal faculties.

This contrasts sharply with Aristotle's hylomorphism, where the soul's form persists as long as the living being exists.

original_claim.warrant: By identifying λόγος as the 'basic character' of Dasein's Being-in-the-world, Heidegger establishes that disclosure is not a property or faculty of a subject but the very structure of Dasein's existence. The terms 'uncovered' and 'exhibited' (related to aletheia as unconcealment) indicate that Erschlossenheit is the condition for the possibility of entities showing themselves. This differs from a representational model where a subject apprehends external objects; instead, Dasein's Being is constituted by its openness to beings, and this openness is structured by λόγος as the articulative dimension of understanding.
original_claim.backing: The emphasis on 'hearing-saying' (λέγειν) as the source of knowledge reinforces that disclosure is fundamentally interpretive and linguistic, not merely perceptual. original_claim.claim: Both Aristotelian phantasia and Heideggerian Erschlossenheit function as pre-predicative modes of disclosure that enable access to beings prior to explicit judgment, establishing structural parallels in their mediating roles between immediate presence and conceptual determination.
grounds: Aristotle's phantasia operates as 'making-present-to-itself' of what is 'not actually there,' functioning before propositional judgment.

Heidegger describes a mode of disclosure where 'there is for uncovering no possibility of dissimulating, of mis-leading,' suggesting a primordial access to beings that precedes the possibility of error inherent in propositional assertion.

Both frameworks position their respective disclosure mechanisms as mediating structures: phantasia between perception and thought in Aristotle, and Erschlossenheit as the existential condition for any particular acts of knowing in Heidegger.
original_claim.warrant: The structural parallel lies in how both concepts establish a level of disclosure that is more fundamental than propositional knowledge yet more articulated than mere sensation. Phantasia's 'making-present' of absent objects and Erschlossenheit's primordial 'uncovering' both describe modes of access that are not reducible to either pure receptivity or conceptual judgment. This pre-predicative character is crucial because it establishes the conditions for the possibility of truth and falsity in judgment—one cannot make true or false assertions about beings unless those beings are already disclosed in some way.
original_claim.backing: The impossibility of 'dissimulating' in primordial uncovering suggests that Heidegger, like Aristotle with phantasia's pre-doxastic character, recognizes a mode of disclosure that is prior to the subject-predicate structure where error becomes possible. This aligns with phenomenological emphasis on pre-theoretical experience.
original_claim.qualification: The parallel is structural rather than historical; there is limited evidence that Heidegger explicitly derived Erschlossenheit from Aristotelian phantasia, though his extensive engagement with Aristotle suggests implicit influence.

This commits Aristotle to a view where disclosure happens through the actualization of specific psychic powers in relation to their objects, maintaining a distinction between the soul as subject and the world as object, even while unified through hylomorphic composition.
original_claim.backing: The integration of appetite within the sensitive power demonstrates Aristotle's systematic approach to psychic faculties as interconnected yet distinct, each contributing to the soul's overall functioning. original_claim.claim: Heidegger's existential analytic fundamentally diverges from Aristotelian faculty psychology by rejecting substance ontology and reconceiving Dasein not as a being with properties or faculties but as existence whose Being is constituted by its 'being-there' (Da-sein), thereby dissolving the inner-outer distinction presupposed by representational models of disclosure.
grounds: Heidegger characterizes human existence as 'being-there' where 'the being whose being constitutes the τί ἤν εἶναι is designated as ἕκαστον, "the particular," the τί ἤν εἶναι constitutes the particularity of beings,' reinterpreting Aristotelian essence in existential terms.
The concept of Dasein as potentially 'become "no-longer-Being-there" [Nicht-mehr-da-sein]' emphasizes existence as temporal and finite rather than as a substance with enduring properties.

Heidegger's framework involves 'temporality' as fundamental, where 'to say that it is something which is "earlier" and "later", "not yet" and "no longer"' structures Dasein's Being, contrasting with Aristotle's atemporal account of psychic faculties.
original_claim.warrant: By reconceiving the human being as Dasein—literally 'being-there'—Heidegger shifts from asking 'what is the soul?' to 'how does Dasein exist?' This existential approach dissolves the subject-object framework that structures Aristotelian faculty psychology. Where Aristotle's phantasia mediates between an external world and an internal soul through images, Heidegger's Erschlossenheit is the very structure of Dasein's Being-in-the-world, eliminating the need for mediation. The emphasis on temporality as constitutive of Dasein's Being further distinguishes Heidegger's approach from Aristotle's analysis of timeless psychic capacities, making disclosure fundamentally historical and finite rather than a function of universal faculties.
original_claim.backing: The possibility of Dasein's 'no-longer-Being-there' (death) is not merely the cessation of a substance but belongs to Dasein's Being as such, revealing how existence rather than essence structures Heidegger's ontology. This contrasts sharply with Aristotle's hylomorphism, where the soul's form persists as long as the living being exists.
original_claim.rebuttal: One might argue that Aristotle's hylomorphism already overcomes Cartesian dualism by unifying soul and body, but Heidegger would respond that even hylomorphism retains a substance ontology that his existential analytic seeks to overcome.

original_claim.claim: Aristotle's phantasia functions as a mediating faculty that discloses appearances (phainomena) through a process of 'making-present-to-itself' that operates independently of immediate sensory presence, thereby enabling thought to engage with objects not currently perceived.
grounds: Heidegger characterizes Aristotelian thinking as 'not an appeal to a brain process, but to φαντασία, the "making-present-to-itself" of the world, in which what is made present is not actually there, but instead is, say, in memory.'
Aristotle's account acknowledges that 'theoretical reasoning cannot do without "images"' (phantasmata), indicating phantasia's indispensable role in cognitive operations.
Scholarly interpretations by Modrak and Nussbaum present 'competing but equally compelling readings of Aristotelian phantasia as a crucial part of the meaning-making process.'
original_claim.warrant: The characterization of phantasia as 'making-present-to-itself' reveals its function as a disclosure mechanism that transcends the immediate givenness of perception. By enabling the soul to engage with absent objects through retained images, phantasia establishes a mode of access to beings that is neither purely sensory nor purely intellectual, but mediates between these domains. This mediating function constitutes a form of disclosure because it makes phenomena available to consciousness in a way that enables further cognitive operations, particularly thinking and deliberation.
original_claim.backing: The necessity of images for theoretical reasoning demonstrates that phantasia is not merely auxiliary to cognition but constitutive of it. The scholarly recognition of phantasia's role in meaning-making further supports its status as a disclosure faculty rather than a passive repository of sensory residues.
original_claim.qualification: This interpretation depends on Heidegger's phenomenological reading of Aristotle, which may emphasize aspects of phantasia that Aristotle himself did not explicitly thematize as 'disclosure.'

original_claim.claim: Heidegger's Erschlossenheit structures the disclosure of Being-in-the-world by constituting Dasein as fundamentally characterized by λόγος, which governs how beings are 'uncovered' and 'exhibited' within the existential 'there' (Da) of Dasein's being.
grounds: Heidegger explicates 'the being-there of the human being as being-in-the-world, in such a way that λόγος came forth as the basic character of this being, determined as being-in: the how of this being.'
In Heidegger's framework, 'as λόγος is what governs, I draw my knowledge from hearing-saying,' indicating that disclosure operates through linguistic and interpretive structures.
The process of disclosure involves beings being 'uncovered, exhibited,' suggesting that Erschlossenheit is not passive reception but active unconcealment.
original_claim.warrant: By identifying λόγος as the 'basic character' of Dasein's Being-in-the-world, Heidegger establishes that disclosure is not a property or faculty of a subject but the very structure of Dasein's existence. The terms 'uncovered' and 'exhibited' (related to aletheia as unconcealment) indicate that Erschlossenheit is the condition for the possibility of entities showing themselves. This differs from a representational model where a subject apprehends external objects; instead, Dasein's Being is constituted by its openness to beings, and this openness is structured by λόγος as the articulative dimension of understanding.
original_claim.backing: The emphasis on 'hearing-saying' (λέγειν) as the source of knowledge reinforces that disclosure is fundamentally interpretive and linguistic, not merely perceptual. This aligns with Heidegger's analysis of discourse (Rede) as one of the constitutive existentials of Erschlossenheit.

original_claim.claim: Both Aristotelian phantasia and Heideggerian Erschlossenheit function as pre-predicative modes of disclosure that enable access to beings prior to explicit judgment, establishing structural parallels in their mediating roles between immediate presence and conceptual determination.
grounds: Aristotle's phantasia operates as 'making-present-to-itself' of what is 'not actually there,' functioning before propositional judgment.

Heidegger describes a mode of disclosure where 'there is for uncovering no possibility of dissimulating, of mis-leading,' suggesting a primordial access to beings that precedes the possibility of error inherent in propositional assertion.

Both frameworks position their respective disclosure mechanisms as mediating structures: phantasia between perception and thought in Aristotle, and Erschlossenheit as the existential condition for any particular acts of knowing in Heidegger.
original_claim.warrant: The structural parallel lies in how both concepts establish a level of disclosure that is more fundamental than propositional knowledge yet more articulated than mere sensation. Phantasia's 'making-present' of absent objects and Erschlossenheit's primordial 'uncovering' both describe modes of access that are not reducible to either pure receptivity or conceptual judgment. This pre-predicative character is crucial because it establishes the conditions for the possibility of truth and falsity in judgment—one cannot make true or false assertions about beings unless those beings are already disclosed in some way.
original_claim.backing: The impossibility of 'dissimulating' in primordial uncovering suggests that Heidegger, like Aristotle with phantasia's pre-doxastic character, recognizes a mode of disclosure that is prior to the subject-predicate structure where error becomes possible. This aligns with phenomenological emphasis on pre-theoretical experience.
original_claim.qualification: The parallel is structural rather than historical; there is limited evidence that Heidegger explicitly derived Erschlossenheit from Aristotelian phantasia, though his extensive engagement with Aristotle suggests implicit influence.

original_claim.claim: Despite their structural parallels in establishing pre-predicative disclosure, the fundamental divergence between Aristotelian phantasia and Heideggerian Erschlossenheit reflects the broader methodological shift from ancient faculty psychology's analysis of psychic powers to phenomenological existential analytic's interrogation of the meaning of Being itself.
grounds: Aristotle's approach involves analyzing 'what the task of the φυσικός, with regard to the ψυχή, genuinely is,' situating his inquiry within natural philosophy's investigation of the soul as a natural entity.

Heidegger's method, by contrast, emphasizes that 'the previous characterization of temporality is not only quite incomplete in that we have not paid attention to all the dimensions of this phenomenon; it also is defective in principle,' indicating an ongoing phenomenological interrogation rather than a systematic catalog of faculties.

The interpretive tradition shows that Heidegger's engagement with Aristotle involves retrieval and transformation: scholarly work on 'Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotle' reveals how phenomenology reinterprets ancient concepts within a fundamentally different ontological framework.
original_claim.warrant: The methodological divergence is not merely a difference in terminology but reflects fundamentally different philosophical projects. Aristotle's inquiry into phantasia serves his broader investigation of the soul as a natural form, seeking to identify and distinguish the various capacities that constitute psychic life. Heidegger's analysis of Erschlossenheit, however, is not aimed at cataloging existential structures but at uncovering the meaning of Being through an analysis of the being (Dasein) for whom Being is an issue. This shift from 'what is the soul?' to 'what does it mean to be?' transforms how disclosure is understood—from a faculty's operation to the very structure of existence itself.
original_claim.backing: The acknowledgment that Heidegger's characterization remains 'incomplete' and 'defective in principle' reveals phenomenology's hermeneutic character, where understanding is always provisional and subject to deeper interrogation. original_claim.qualification: This divergence does not necessarily imply that Heidegger's approach is superior; rather, it reflects different philosophical aims and contexts—ancient natural philosophy versus modern phenomenological ontology.

original_claim.claim: Aristotle's phantasia functions as a mediating faculty that discloses appearances (phainomena) through a process of 'making-present-to-itself' that operates independently of immediate sensory presence, thereby enabling thought to engage with objects not currently perceived.
grounds: Heidegger characterizes Aristotelian thinking as 'not an appeal to a brain process, but to φαντασία, the "making-present-to-itself" of the world, in which what is made present is not actually there, but instead is, say, in memory.'
Aristotle's account acknowledges that 'theoretical reasoning cannot do without "images"' (phantasmata), indicating phantasia's indispensable role in cognitive operations.
Scholarly interpretations by Modrak and Nussbaum present 'competing but equally compelling readings of Aristotelian phantasia as a crucial part of the meaning-making process.'
original_claim.warrant: The characterization of phantasia as 'making-present-to-itself' reveals its function as a disclosure mechanism that transcends the immediate givenness of perception. By enabling the soul to engage with absent objects through retained images, phantasia establishes a mode of access to beings that is neither purely sensory nor purely intellectual, but mediates between these domains. This mediating function constitutes a form of disclosure because it makes phenomena available to consciousness in a way that enables further cognitive operations, particularly thinking and deliberation.
original_claim.backing: The necessity of images for theoretical reasoning demonstrates that phantasia is not merely auxiliary to cognition but constitutive of it. The scholarly recognition of phantasia's role in meaning-making further supports its status as a disclosure faculty rather than a passive repository of sensory residues.
original_claim.qualification: This interpretation depends on Heidegger's phenomenological reading of Aristotle, which may emphasize aspects of phantasia that Aristotle himself did not explicitly thematize as 'disclosure.'

original_claim.claim: Heidegger's Erschlossenheit structures the disclosure of Being-in-the-world by constituting Dasein as fundamentally characterized by λόγος, which governs how beings are 'uncovered' and 'exhibited' within the existential 'there' (Da) of Dasein's being.
grounds: Heidegger explicates 'the being-there of the human being as being-in-the-world, in such a way that λόγος came forth as the basic character of this being, determined as being-in: the how of this being.'
In Heidegger's framework, 'as λόγος is what governs, I draw my knowledge from hearing-saying,' indicating that disclosure operates through linguistic and interpretive structures.
The process of disclosure involves beings being 'uncovered, exhibited,' suggesting that Erschlossenheit is not passive reception but active unconcealment.
original_claim.warrant: By identifying λόγος as the 'basic character' of Dasein's Being-in-the-world, Heidegger establishes that disclosure is not a property or faculty of a subject but the very structure of Dasein's existence. The terms 'uncovered' and 'exhibited' (related to aletheia as unconcealment) indicate that Erschlossenheit is the condition for the possibility of entities showing themselves. This differs from a representational model where a subject apprehends external objects; instead, Dasein's Being is constituted by its openness to beings, and this openness is structured by λόγος as the articulative dimension of understanding.
original_claim.backing: The emphasis on 'hearing-saying' (λέγειν) as the source of knowledge reinforces that disclosure is fundamentally interpretive and linguistic, not merely perceptual. This aligns with Heidegger's analysis of discourse (Rede) as one of the constitutive existentials of Erschlossenheit.

original_claim.claim: Both Aristotelian phantasia and Heideggerian Erschlossenheit function as pre-predicative modes of disclosure that enable access to beings prior to explicit judgment, establishing structural parallels in their mediating roles between immediate presence and conceptual determination.
grounds: Aristotle's phantasia operates as 'making-present-to-itself' of what is 'not actually there,' functioning before propositional judgment.

Heidegger describes a mode of disclosure where 'there is for uncovering no possibility of dissimulating, of mis-leading,' suggesting a primordial access to beings that precedes the possibility of error inherent in propositional assertion.

Both frameworks position their respective disclosure mechanisms as mediating structures: phantasia between perception and thought in Aristotle, and Erschlossenheit as the existential condition for any particular acts of knowing in Heidegger.
original_claim.warrant: The structural parallel lies in how both concepts establish a level of disclosure that is more fundamental than propositional knowledge yet more articulated than mere sensation. Phantasia's 'making-present' of absent objects and Erschlossenheit's primordial 'uncovering' both describe modes of access that are not reducible to either pure receptivity or conceptual judgment. This pre-predicative character is crucial because it establishes the conditions for the possibility of truth and falsity in judgment—one cannot make true or false assertions about beings unless those beings are already disclosed in some way.
original_claim.backing: The impossibility of 'dissimulating' in primordial uncovering suggests that Heidegger, like Aristotle with phantasia's pre-doxastic character, recognizes a mode of disclosure that is prior to the subject-predicate structure where error becomes possible. This aligns with phenomenological emphasis on pre-theoretical experience.
original_claim.qualification: The parallel is structural rather than historical; there is limited evidence that Heidegger explicitly derived Erschlossenheit from Aristotelian phantasia, though his extensive engagement with Aristotle suggests implicit influence.

original_claim.claim: Heidegger's existential analytic fundamentally diverges from Aristotelian faculty psychology by rejecting substance ontology and reconceiving Dasein not as a being with properties or faculties but as existence whose Being is constituted by its 'being-there' (Da-sein), thereby dissolving the inner-outer distinction presupposed by representational models of disclosure.
grounds: Heidegger characterizes human existence as 'being-there' where 'the being whose being constitutes the τί ἤν εἶναι is designated as ἕκαστον, "the particular," the τί ἤν εἶναι constitutes the particularity of beings,' reinterpreting Aristotelian essence in existential terms.
The concept of Dasein as potentially 'become "no-longer-Being-there" [Nicht-mehr-da-sein]' emphasizes existence as temporal and finite rather than as a substance with enduring properties.

Heidegger's framework involves 'temporality' as fundamental, where 'to say that it is something which is "earlier" and "later", "not yet" and "no longer"' structures Dasein's Being, contrasting with Aristotle's atemporal account of psychic faculties.
original_claim.warrant: By reconceiving the human being as Dasein—literally 'being-there'—Heidegger shifts from asking 'what is the soul?' to 'how does Dasein exist?' This existential approach dissolves the subject-object framework that structures Aristotelian faculty psychology. Where Aristotle's phantasia mediates between an external world and an internal soul through images, Heidegger's Erschlossenheit is the very structure of Dasein's Being-in-the-world, eliminating the need for mediation. The emphasis on temporality as constitutive of Dasein's Being further distinguishes Heidegger's approach from Aristotle's analysis of timeless psychic capacities, making disclosure fundamentally historical and finite rather than a function of universal faculties.
original_claim.backing: The possibility of Dasein's 'no-longer-Being-there' (death) is not merely the cessation of a substance but belongs to Dasein's Being as such, revealing how existence rather than essence structures Heidegger's ontology. This contrasts sharply with Aristotle's hylomorphism, where the soul's form persists as long as the living being exists.
original_claim.rebuttal: One might argue that Aristotle's hylomorphism already overcomes Cartesian dualism by unifying soul and body, but Heidegger would respond that even hylomorphism retains a substance ontology that his existential analytic seeks to overcome.

original_claim.claim: Despite their structural parallels in establishing pre-predicative disclosure, the fundamental divergence between Aristotelian phantasia and Heideggerian Erschlossenheit reflects the broader methodological shift from ancient faculty psychology's analysis of psychic powers to phenomenological existential analytic's interrogation of the meaning of Being itself.
grounds: Aristotle's approach involves analyzing 'what the task of the φυσικός, with regard to the ψυχή, genuinely is,' situating his inquiry within natural philosophy's investigation of the soul as a natural entity.

Heidegger's method, by contrast, emphasizes that 'the previous characterization of temporality is not only quite incomplete in that we have not paid attention to all the dimensions of this phenomenon; it also is defective in principle,' indicating an ongoing phenomenological interrogation rather than a systematic catalog of faculties.

The interpretive tradition shows that Heidegger's engagement with Aristotle involves retrieval and transformation: scholarly work on 'Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotle' reveals how phenomenology reinterprets ancient concepts within a fundamentally different ontological framework.
original_claim.warrant: The methodological divergence is not merely a difference in terminology but reflects fundamentally different philosophical projects. Aristotle's inquiry into phantasia serves his broader investigation of the soul as a natural form, seeking to identify and distinguish the various capacities that constitute psychic life. Heidegger's analysis of Erschlossenheit, however, is not aimed at cataloging existential structures but at uncovering the meaning of Being through an analysis of the being (Dasein) for whom Being is an issue. This shift from 'what is the soul?' to 'what does it mean to be?' transforms how disclosure is understood—from a faculty's operation to the very structure of existence itself.
original_claim.backing: The acknowledgment that Heidegger's characterization remains 'incomplete' and 'defective in principle' reveals phenomenology's hermeneutic character, where understanding is always provisional and subject to deeper interrogation. This contrasts with Aristotle's more systematic and definitive approach to defining psychic faculties.
original_claim.qualification: This divergence does not necessarily imply that Heidegger's approach is superior; rather, it reflects different philosophical aims and contexts—ancient natural philosophy versus modern phenomenological ontology.

original_claim.claim: Aristotle's phantasia functions as a mediating faculty that discloses appearances (phainomena) through a process of 'making-present-to-itself' that operates independently of immediate sensory presence, thereby enabling thought to engage with objects not currently perceived.
grounds: Heidegger characterizes Aristotelian thinking as 'not an appeal to a brain process, but to φαντασία, the "making-present-to-itself" of the world, in which what is made present is not actually there, but instead is, say, in memory.'
Aristotle's account acknowledges that 'theoretical reasoning cannot do without "images"' (phantasmata), indicating phantasia's indispensable role in cognitive operations.
Scholarly interpretations by Modrak and Nussbaum present 'competing but equally compelling readings of Aristotelian phantasia as a crucial part of the meaning-making process.'
original_claim.warrant: The characterization of phantasia as 'making-present-to-itself' reveals its function as a disclosure mechanism that transcends the immediate givenness of perception. By enabling the soul to engage with absent objects through retained images, phantasia establishes a mode of access to beings that is neither purely sensory nor purely intellectual, but mediates between these domains. This mediating function constitutes a form of disclosure because it makes phenomena available to consciousness in a way that enables further cognitive operations, particularly thinking and deliberation.
original_claim.backing: The necessity of images for theoretical reasoning demonstrates that phantasia is not merely auxiliary to cognition but constitutive of it. The scholarly recognition of phantasia's role in meaning-making further supports its status as a disclosure faculty rather than a passive repository of sensory residues.
original_claim.qualification: This interpretation depends on Heidegger's phenomenological reading of Aristotle, which may emphasize aspects of phantasia that Aristotle himself did not explicitly thematize as 'disclosure.'

original_claim.claim: Heidegger's Erschlossenheit structures the disclosure of Being-in-the-world by constituting Dasein as fundamentally characterized by λόγος, which governs how beings are 'uncovered' and 'exhibited' within the existential 'there' (Da) of Dasein's being.
grounds: Heidegger explicates 'the being-there of the human being as being-in-the-world, in such a way that λόγος came forth as the basic character of this being, determined as being-in: the how of this being.'
In Heidegger's framework, 'as λόγος is what governs, I draw my knowledge from hearing-saying,' indicating that disclosure operates through linguistic and interpretive structures.
The process of disclosure involves beings being 'uncovered, exhibited,' suggesting that Erschlossenheit is not passive reception but active unconcealment.
original_claim.warrant: By identifying λόγος as the 'basic character' of Dasein's Being-in-the-world, Heidegger establishes that disclosure is not a property or faculty of a subject but the very structure of Dasein's existence. The terms 'uncovered' and 'exhibited' (related to aletheia as unconcealment) indicate that Erschlossenheit is the condition for the possibility of entities showing themselves. This differs from a representational model where a subject apprehends external objects; instead, Dasein's Being is constituted by its openness to beings, and this openness is structured by λόγος as the articulative dimension of understanding.
original_claim.backing: The emphasis on 'hearing-saying' (λέγειν) as the source of knowledge reinforces that disclosure is fundamentally interpretive and linguistic, not merely perceptual. This aligns with Heidegger's analysis of discourse (Rede) as one of the constitutive existentials of Erschlossenheit.

original_claim.claim: Both Aristotelian phantasia and Heideggerian Erschlossenheit function as pre-predicative modes of disclosure that enable access to beings prior to explicit judgment, establishing structural parallels in their mediating roles between immediate presence and conceptual determination.
grounds: Aristotle's phantasia operates as 'making-present-to-itself' of what is 'not actually there,' functioning before propositional judgment.

Heidegger describes a mode of disclosure where 'there is for uncovering no possibility of dissimulating, of mis-leading,' suggesting a primordial access to beings that precedes the possibility of error inherent in propositional assertion.

Both frameworks position their respective disclosure mechanisms as mediating structures: phantasia between perception and thought in Aristotle, and Erschlossenheit as the existential condition for any particular acts of knowing in Heidegger.
original_claim.warrant: The structural parallel lies in how both concepts establish a level of disclosure that is more fundamental than propositional knowledge yet more articulated than mere sensation. Phantasia's 'making-present' of absent objects and Erschlossenheit's primordial 'uncovering' both describe modes of access that are not reducible to either pure receptivity or conceptual judgment. This pre-predicative character is crucial because it establishes the conditions for the possibility of truth and falsity in judgment—one cannot make true or false assertions about beings unless those beings are already disclosed in some way.
original_claim.backing: The impossibility of 'dissimulating' in primordial uncovering suggests that Heidegger, like Aristotle with phantasia's pre-doxastic character, recognizes a mode of disclosure that is prior to the subject-predicate structure where error becomes possible. This aligns with phenomenological emphasis on pre-theoretical experience.
original_claim.qualification: The parallel is structural rather than historical; there is limited evidence that Heidegger explicitly derived Erschlossenheit from Aristotelian phantasia, though his extensive engagement with Aristotle suggests implicit influence.

This framework involves 'a double type of consideration' regarding the soul (ψυχή), reflecting Aristotle's methodological commitment to analyzing the soul through its various faculties and their interrelations.

The concept of κίνησις as 'ἐντελέχεια, "presence," τοῦ δυνάμει ὄντος, "of a determinate being-there"' reveals Aristotle's metaphysical framework of potentiality and actuality structuring his account of psychic powers.

This commits Aristotle to a view where disclosure happens through the actualization of specific psychic powers in relation to their objects, maintaining a distinction between the soul as subject and the world as object, even while unified through hylomorphic composition.
original_claim.backing: The integration of appetite within the sensitive power demonstrates Aristotle's systematic approach to psychic faculties as interconnected yet distinct, each contributing to the soul's overall functioning. original_claim.claim: Heidegger's existential analytic fundamentally diverges from Aristotelian faculty psychology by rejecting substance ontology and reconceiving Dasein not as a being with properties or faculties but as existence whose Being is constituted by its 'being-there' (Da-sein), thereby dissolving the inner-outer distinction presupposed by representational models of disclosure.
grounds: Heidegger characterizes human existence as 'being-there' where 'the being whose being constitutes the τί ἤν εἶναι is designated as ἕκαστον, "the particular," the τί ἤν εἶναι constitutes the particularity of beings,' reinterpreting Aristotelian essence in existential terms.
The concept of Dasein as potentially 'become "no-longer-Being-there" [Nicht-mehr-da-sein]' emphasizes existence as temporal and finite rather than as a substance with enduring properties.

Heidegger's framework involves 'temporality' as fundamental, where 'to say that it is something which is "earlier" and "later", "not yet" and "no longer"' structures Dasein's Being, contrasting with Aristotle's atemporal account of psychic faculties.
original_claim.warrant: By reconceiving the human being as Dasein—literally 'being-there'—Heidegger shifts from asking 'what is the soul?' to 'how does Dasein exist?' This existential approach dissolves the subject-object framework that structures Aristotelian faculty psychology. Where Aristotle's phantasia mediates between an external world and an internal soul through images, Heidegger's Erschlossenheit is the very structure of Dasein's Being-in-the-world, eliminating the need for mediation. The emphasis on temporality as constitutive of Dasein's Being further distinguishes Heidegger's approach from Aristotle's analysis of timeless psychic capacities, making disclosure fundamentally historical and finite rather than a function of universal faculties.
original_claim.backing: The possibility of Dasein's 'no-longer-Being-there' (death) is not merely the cessation of a substance but belongs to Dasein's Being as such, revealing how existence rather than essence structures Heidegger's ontology. This contrasts sharply with Aristotle's hylomorphism, where the soul's form persists as long as the living being exists.
original_claim.rebuttal: One might argue that Aristotle's hylomorphism already overcomes Cartesian dualism by unifying soul and body, but Heidegger would respond that even hylomorphism retains a substance ontology that his existential analytic seeks to overcome.

original_claim.claim: Despite their structural parallels in establishing pre-predicative disclosure, the fundamental divergence between Aristotelian phantasia and Heideggerian Erschlossenheit reflects the broader methodological shift from ancient faculty psychology's analysis of psychic powers to phenomenological existential analytic's interrogation of the meaning of Being itself.
grounds: Aristotle's approach involves analyzing 'what the task of the φυσικός, with regard to the ψυχή, genuinely is,' situating his inquiry within natural philosophy's investigation of the soul as a natural entity.

Heidegger's method, by contrast, emphasizes that 'the previous characterization of temporality is not only quite incomplete in that we have not paid attention to all the dimensions of this phenomenon; it also is defective in principle,' indicating an ongoing phenomenological interrogation rather than a systematic catalog of faculties.

The interpretive tradition shows that Heidegger's engagement with Aristotle involves retrieval and transformation: scholarly work on 'Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotle' reveals how phenomenology reinterprets ancient concepts within a fundamentally different ontological framework.
original_claim.warrant: The methodological divergence is not merely a difference in terminology but reflects fundamentally different philosophical projects. Aristotle's inquiry into phantasia serves his broader investigation of the soul as a natural form, seeking to identify and distinguish the various capacities that constitute psychic life. Heidegger's analysis of Erschlossenheit, however, is not aimed at cataloging existential structures but at uncovering the meaning of Being through an analysis of the being (Dasein) for whom Being is an issue. This shift from 'what is the soul?' to 'what does it mean to be?' transforms how disclosure is understood—from a faculty's operation to the very structure of existence itself.
original_claim.backing: The acknowledgment that Heidegger's characterization remains 'incomplete' and 'defective in principle' reveals phenomenology's hermeneutic character, where understanding is always provisional and subject to deeper interrogation. This contrasts with Aristotle's more systematic and definitive approach to defining psychic faculties.
original_claim.qualification: This divergence does not necessarily imply that Heidegger's approach is superior; rather, it reflects different philosophical aims and contexts—ancient natural philosophy versus modern phenomenological ontology.

original_claim.claim: Aristotle's phantasia functions as a mediating faculty that discloses appearances (phainomena) through a process of 'making-present-to-itself' that operates independently of immediate sensory presence, thereby enabling thought to engage with objects not currently perceived.
grounds: Heidegger characterizes Aristotelian thinking as 'not an appeal to a brain process, but to φαντασία, the "making-present-to-itself" of the world, in which what is made present is not actually there, but instead is, say, in memory.'
Aristotle's account acknowledges that 'theoretical reasoning cannot do without "images"' (phantasmata), indicating phantasia's indispensable role in cognitive operations.
Scholarly interpretations by Modrak and Nussbaum present 'competing but equally compelling readings of Aristotelian phantasia as a crucial part of the meaning-making process.'
original_claim.warrant: The characterization of phantasia as 'making-present-to-itself' reveals its function as a disclosure mechanism that transcends the immediate givenness of perception. By enabling the soul to engage with absent objects through retained images, phantasia establishes a mode of access to beings that is neither purely sensory nor purely intellectual, but mediates between these domains. This mediating function constitutes a form of disclosure because it makes phenomena available to consciousness in a way that enables further cognitive operations, particularly thinking and deliberation.
original_claim.backing: The necessity of images for theoretical reasoning demonstrates that phantasia is not merely auxiliary to cognition but constitutive of it. The scholarly recognition of phantasia's role in meaning-making further supports its status as a disclosure faculty rather than a passive repository of sensory residues.

original_claim.claim: Heidegger's Erschlossenheit structures the disclosure of Being-in-the-world by constituting Dasein as fundamentally characterized by λόγος, which governs how beings are 'uncovered' and 'exhibited' within the existential 'there' (Da) of Dasein's being.
grounds: Heidegger explicates 'the being-there of the human being as being-in-the-world, in such a way that λόγος came forth as the basic character of this being, determined as being-in: the how of this being.'
In Heidegger's framework, 'as λόγος is what governs, I draw my knowledge from hearing-saying,' indicating that disclosure operates through linguistic and interpretive structures.
The process of disclosure involves beings being 'uncovered, exhibited,' suggesting that Erschlossenheit is not passive reception but active unconcealment.
original_claim.warrant: By identifying λόγος as the 'basic character' of Dasein's Being-in-the-world, Heidegger establishes that disclosure is not a property or faculty of a subject but the very structure of Dasein's existence. The terms 'uncovered' and 'exhibited' (related to aletheia as unconcealment) indicate that Erschlossenheit is the condition for the possibility of entities showing themselves. This differs from a representational model where a subject apprehends external objects; instead, Dasein's Being is constituted by its openness to beings, and this openness is structured by λόγος as the articulative dimension of understanding.
original_claim.backing: The emphasis on 'hearing-saying' (λέγειν) as the source of knowledge reinforces that disclosure is fundamentally interpretive and linguistic, not merely perceptual. This aligns with Heidegger's analysis of discourse (Rede) as one of the constitutive existentials of Erschlossenheit.

original_claim.claim: Both Aristotelian phantasia and Heideggerian Erschlossenheit function as pre-predicative modes of disclosure that enable access to beings prior to explicit judgment, establishing structural parallels in their mediating roles between immediate presence and conceptual determination.
grounds: Aristotle's phantasia operates as 'making-present-to-itself' of what is 'not actually there,' functioning before propositional judgment.

Heidegger describes a mode of disclosure where 'there is for uncovering no possibility of dissimulating, of mis-leading,' suggesting a primordial access to beings that precedes the possibility of error inherent in propositional assertion.

Both frameworks position their respective disclosure mechanisms as mediating structures: phantasia between perception and thought in Aristotle, and Erschlossenheit as the existential condition for any particular acts of knowing in Heidegger.
original_claim.warrant: The structural parallel lies in how both concepts establish a level of disclosure that is more fundamental than propositional knowledge yet more articulated than mere sensation. Phantasia's 'making-present' of absent objects and Erschlossenheit's primordial 'uncovering' both describe modes of access that are not reducible to either pure receptivity or conceptual judgment. This pre-predicative character is crucial because it establishes the conditions for the possibility of truth and falsity in judgment—one cannot make true or false assertions about beings unless those beings are already disclosed in some way.
original_claim.backing: The impossibility of 'dissimulating' in primordial uncovering suggests that Heidegger, like Aristotle with phantasia's pre-doxastic character, recognizes a mode of disclosure that is prior to the subject-predicate structure where error becomes possible. This aligns with phenomenological emphasis on pre-theoretical experience.
original_claim.qualification: The parallel is structural rather than historical; there is limited evidence that Heidegger explicitly derived Erschlossenheit from Aristotelian phantasia, though his extensive engagement with Aristotle suggests implicit influence.

original_claim.claim: Aristotle's phantasia remains embedded within a faculty psychology that presupposes distinct powers (dynameis) of the soul, including the relationship between 'the appetitive power (ὀρεκτικόν)' as 'part of the sensitive power (αἰσθητικόν),' thereby maintaining a hylomorphic framework of soul-body unity.
grounds: Aristotle's analysis establishes that 'the appetitive power (ὀρεκτικόν) is part of the sensitive power (αἰσθητικόν) or that the possession of the sensitive faculty involves the possession' of appetite.

This framework involves 'a double type of consideration' regarding the soul (ψυχή), reflecting Aristotle's methodological commitment to analyzing the soul through its various faculties and their interrelations.

The concept of κίνησις as 'ἐντελέχεια, "presence," τοῦ δυνάμει ὄντος, "of a determinate being-there"' reveals Aristotle's metaphysical framework of potentiality and actuality structuring his account of psychic powers.
original_claim.warrant: Aristotle's faculty psychology operates within a substance ontology where the soul is understood as the form (eidos) of a living body, with distinct capacities or powers that are hierarchically organized and functionally differentiated. Phantasia, within this framework, is one faculty among others (perception, appetite, intellect), each with its proper object and operation. This commits Aristotle to a view where disclosure happens through the actualization of specific psychic powers in relation to their objects, maintaining a distinction between the soul as subject and the world as object, even while unified through hylomorphic composition.
original_claim.backing: The integration of appetite within the sensitive power demonstrates Aristotle's systematic approach to psychic faculties as interconnected yet distinct, each contributing to the soul's overall functioning. The potentiality-actuality framework further grounds this in a broader metaphysical system.

original_claim.claim: Heidegger's existential analytic fundamentally diverges from Aristotelian faculty psychology by rejecting substance ontology and reconceiving Dasein not as a being with properties or faculties but as existence whose Being is constituted by its 'being-there' (Da-sein), thereby dissolving the inner-outer distinction presupposed by representational models of disclosure.
grounds: Heidegger characterizes human existence as 'being-there' where 'the being whose being constitutes the τί ἤν εἶναι is designated as ἕκαστον, "the particular," the τί ἤν εἶναι constitutes the particularity of beings,' reinterpreting Aristotelian essence in existential terms.
The concept of Dasein as potentially 'become "no-longer-Being-there" [Nicht-mehr-da-sein]' emphasizes existence as temporal and finite rather than as a substance with enduring properties.

Heidegger's framework involves 'temporality' as fundamental, where 'to say that it is something which is "earlier" and "later", "not yet" and "no longer"' structures Dasein's Being, contrasting with Aristotle's atemporal account of psychic faculties.
original_claim.warrant: By reconceiving the human being as Dasein—literally 'being-there'—Heidegger shifts from asking 'what is the soul?' to 'how does Dasein exist?' This existential approach dissolves the subject-object framework that structures Aristotelian faculty psychology. Where Aristotle's phantasia mediates between an external world and an internal soul through images, Heidegger's Erschlossenheit is the very structure of Dasein's Being-in-the-world, eliminating the need for mediation. The emphasis on temporality as constitutive of Dasein's Being further distinguishes Heidegger's approach from Aristotle's analysis of timeless psychic capacities, making disclosure fundamentally historical and finite rather than a function of universal faculties.
original_claim.backing: The possibility of Dasein's 'no-longer-Being-there' (death) is not merely the cessation of a substance but belongs to Dasein's Being as such, revealing how existence rather than essence structures Heidegger's ontology. This contrasts sharply with Aristotle's hylomorphism, where the soul's form persists as long as the living being exists.
original_claim.rebuttal: One might argue that Aristotle's hylomorphism already overcomes Cartesian dualism by unifying soul and body, but Heidegger would respond that even hylomorphism retains a substance ontology that his existential analytic seeks to overcome.

original_claim.claim: Despite their structural parallels in establishing pre-predicative disclosure, the fundamental divergence between Aristotelian phantasia and Heideggerian Erschlossenheit reflects the broader methodological shift from ancient faculty psychology's analysis of psychic powers to phenomenological existential analytic's interrogation of the meaning of Being itself.
grounds: Aristotle's approach involves analyzing 'what the task of the φυσικός, with regard to the ψυχή, genuinely is,' situating his inquiry within natural philosophy's investigation of the soul as a natural entity.

Heidegger's method, by contrast, emphasizes that 'the previous characterization of temporality is not only quite incomplete in that we have not paid attention to all the dimensions of this phenomenon; it also is defective in principle,' indicating an ongoing phenomenological interrogation rather than a systematic catalog of faculties.

The interpretive tradition shows that Heidegger's engagement with Aristotle involves retrieval and transformation: scholarly work on 'Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotle' reveals how phenomenology reinterprets ancient concepts within a fundamentally different ontological framework.
original_claim.warrant: The methodological divergence is not merely a difference in terminology but reflects fundamentally different philosophical projects. Aristotle's inquiry into phantasia serves his broader investigation of the soul as a natural form, seeking to identify and distinguish the various capacities that constitute psychic life. Heidegger's analysis of Erschlossenheit, however, is not aimed at cataloging existential structures but at uncovering the meaning of Being through an analysis of the being (Dasein) for whom Being is an issue.
